title: Discontinuation of statins in routine care settings.
text_summary: 本研究旨在探讨阿达木单抗治疗中度至重度痤疮丙酸杆菌病的效果。通过一项随机对照试验，研究人员发现阿达木单抗在改善患者症状方面具有显著疗效。具体而言，试验结果显示，接受阿达木单抗治疗的患者在16周时达到临床反应的比例显著高于安慰剂组。此外，研究还发现，阿达木单抗治疗可显著减少患者炎症结节和斑块的数量。然而，部分研究人员对试验方法提出了质疑，认为试验存在终点指标变化过多、样本量不足等问题。针对这些质疑，研究团队进行了回应，解释了终点指标变化的原因，并强调试验结果的有效性。总之，本研究证实了阿达木单抗在治疗中度至重度痤疮丙酸杆菌病方面的有效性，为临床治疗提供了新的选择。

COMMENTS AND RESPONSES
Treatment of Moderate to Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa
TO THE EDITOR: The phase 2 randomized trial by Kimball and
colleagues (1), which claims a beneﬁt of adalimumab in hidradenitis
suppurativa, raises numerous questions about its methodology his-
tory (2). First, although the authors state that the primary outcome
was “prespeciﬁed,” the trial’s history of changes on ClinicalTrials.gov
notes substantial alterations on 7 May 2011, more than 2 years after
the trial began (3). Speciﬁcally, the primary outcome was altered on
that date from an undeﬁned “Physician’s Global Assessment” to
“Percentage of Participants Achieving Clinical Response at Week
16.” Another primary outcome of “Adverse Events” at a time point
of week 52 was changed to “Percent Change From Baseline in Num-
ber of All Inﬂammatory Nodules and Plaques at Week 16.”
A secondary end point of Physician’s Global Assessment at week
52 was changed to “Percentage of Participants Achieving Clinical
Response at Week 8.” A secondary outcome of “Nodule, Fistula and
Abcess [sic] Improvement,” which was not signiﬁcantly improved
(see Appendix Table 5), was changed to “Percentage of Participants
Achieving Clinical Response at Week 12.” Other alterations oc-
curred, but my question is the same: Do the authors have an expla-
nation for these excessive late changes?
In addition, on 12 November 2009, the authors changed the
dose of group 2 from “40 mg eow (end of week) through Week 15”
to “40 mg eow (every other week) through Week 15” (4), preserving
the acronym “eow” while changing its meaning. I admittedly do not
understand the original language, because I am not sure how “end of
week” would differ from “Arm 1: weekly.” Can the authors clarify
this as well?
In short, in the absence of a satisfying explanation, this study is
an underpowered randomized phase 2 trial with multiple subjective
and shifting end points. I count at least 7 scales used as primary or
secondary end points. Multiplying by 3 groups and several time
points yields a minimum of 40 possible comparisons that could be
made. It should not be surprising that some are unsurprising (5).
It may be worth noting that, of 16 authors, 13 disclose conﬂicts
of interest (81%), whereas 1 author’s International Committee of
Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) form was inaccessible to me. Fi-
nally, the authors note that the study protocol and data set are not
available; I urge them to post this information publicly.
Vinay Prasad, MD
National Cancer Institute and National Institutes of Health
Bethesda, Maryland
Disclaimer: The views and opinions of the author do not reﬂect those of
the National Institutes of Health.
Potential Conflicts of Interest: None disclosed.
References

Adalimumab for the treatment of moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa: a par-

2. Krumholz HM. Documenting the methods history: would it improve the interpret-
ability of studies? [Editorial]. Circ Cardiovasc Qual Outcomes. 2012;5:418-9. [PMID:
22811497]
3. ClinicalTrials.gov. Changes to NCT00918255 on 2011_05_07. Accessed at http://
clinicaltrials.gov/archive/NCT00918255/2011_05_07/changes on 23 December 2012.
4. ClinicalTrials.gov. Changes to NCT00918255 on 2009_11_12. Accessed at http://
clinicaltrials.gov/archive/NCT00918255/2009_11_12/changes on 23 December 2012.
5. Ioannidis JP. The importance of potential studies that have not existed and regis-
tration of observational data sets. JAMA. 2012;308:575-6. [PMID: 22871867]
IN RESPONSE: Dr. Prasad unfortunately misinterprets clariﬁcations
and a correction of prespeciﬁed end point descriptions in Clinical-
Trials.gov to be “shifting” of the end points themselves in our study
showing the effectiveness of adalimumab in the treatment of moder-
ate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa. These clariﬁcations and cor-
rection do not reﬂect any deviation of study conduct or reporting
from good clinical practice; in fact, some were requested by
ClinicalTrials.gov itself.
The authors afﬁrm that the Physician’s Global Assessment was
the prespeciﬁed instrument used to evaluate the degree of severity of
study patients with hidradenitis suppurativa. The protocol-deﬁned
prespeciﬁed primary end point has always been the percentage of
patients achieving clinical response at week 16. We further afﬁrm
that clinical response was assessed using the Physician’s Global As-
sessment instrument and was deﬁned as a Physician’s Global Assess-
ment score of clear, minimal, or mild, with at least a 2-grade im-
provement relative to baseline score. The ClinicalTrials.gov posting
that Dr. Prasad mentions was changed to provide more detail about
the primary end point, which remained the same, in the posting.
The description of the secondary end points in ClinicalTrials.gov
was similarly expanded to clarify the protocol-deﬁned prespeciﬁed
end points and to include the time point information, per requests
from ClinicalTrials.gov.
The change in the description of dosing in group 2 from “40
mg eow (end of week)” to “40 mg eow (every other week)” was a
correction of a mistake in the original entry. The error was identiﬁed
and corrected in 2 weeks. The dosing itself in group 2 was prespeci-
ﬁed in the protocol, did not change during study conduct, and is
accurately described in the publication.
The study was powered only for the prespeciﬁed primary end
point (as stated in the Methods section of the publication), not for
secondary end points, and success for this study was assessed using
the primary end point. Evaluation of the primary end point depends
on the count of different types of inﬂammatory lesions as assessed by
the study physicians and is therefore not subjective. As mentioned,
the end point did not shift during the study.
The results from the secondary end points, which measure dif-
ferent dimensions of disease severity than the primary end point,
further support the effectiveness of adalimumab in the treatment of
moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa; these secondary end
points were prespeciﬁed to aid in validation and improvement of the
scoring system for the primary end point.
Each author provided ICMJE forms for conﬂicts of interest
directly to Annals of Internal Medicine, and we refer you back to the
journal for any that are inaccessible. Annals does not currently re-
quire public posting of study protocols or data sets; however, sub-
stantial information, as has been noted, is available at ClinicalTrials
.gov.

Accuracy of Electronically Reported “Meaningful Use”
Clinical Quality Measures
TO THE EDITOR: Let’s face it. Although we can challenge Kern and
colleagues’ (1) methods (for example, by claiming that electronic
health records [EHRs] are much different today than they were in
2008), I don’t think that we can challenge their ﬁndings. The Achil-
les’ heel of end-to-end quality reporting from EHRs lies with data
capture. The challenges to data capture are many—divergent data
requirements (across quality measures, decision support rules, clinical
practice guidelines, and others), time pressures, and skepticism (for
example, are all these data elements really necessary?)—which can
leave providers overwhelmed and resistant.
Quality reporting is required under the federal meaningful use
regulations mandated by the 2009 Health Information Technology
for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act. A meaningful
use–certiﬁed EHR must be able to export standardized quality re-
ports, which can then be fed into a calculation engine to compute
various aggregate scores (such as the number of patients meeting the
numerator and denominator criteria). Interoperability standards for
quality reports have been carefully crafted within the Health Level 7
standards organization and widely vetted, but we have to acknowl-
edge that garbage in equals garbage out and that interoperability
standards that support quality reporting cannot compensate for in-
consistent or missing data at the source.
So, how is the standards community addressing the challenge of
data capture? We are addressing it head-on by providing the deﬁni-
tive source of truth and direction needed by software vendors and
clinicians. Through standardization comes a convergence on key data
elements needed for transitions in care, quality reporting, and deci-
sion support. Rather than having numerous use cases (for example,
transitions of care, clinical decision support, and quality measure-
ment), each with its own data requirements converging on the point-
of-care provider, standardization leads to a convergence of key data
elements. This convergence sets a clearer path for vendors and user
interface designers, lessens the burden of data capture on clinicians,
and focuses data capture on data elements known to be valuable for
various purposes.
In other words, interoperability standards are relevant both on
the afferent and efferent limbs of the EHR. Focusing on standards is
a tractable approach for addressing challenges to data capture and
therefore provides a strategy for addressing the very real challenges
with data quality identiﬁed by Kern and associates.
Robert H. Dolin, MD
Lantana Consulting Group and Health Level 7 International
East Thetford, Vermont
Potential Conflicts of Interest: None disclosed.
Reference
1. Kern LM, Malhotra S, Barro´n Y, Quaresimo J, Dhopeshwarkar R, Pichardo M,
et al. Accuracy of electronically reported “meaningful use” clinical quality measures: a
cross-sectional study. Ann Intern Med. 2013;158:77-83. [PMID: 23318309]
IN RESPONSE: We agree that interoperability standards are a critical
component for improving the accuracy of quality reporting. We
think that other important strategies for improving the accuracy of
quality reporting include changing clinical workﬂow to facilitate doc-
umentation of the care provided, changing EHRs to create new
structured ﬁelds for important variables previously captured only by
free text, improving speciﬁcations for automated reporting of quality
measures, and testing the accuracy of those speciﬁcations. These
strategies do not need to be pursued in sequence; rather, they can
and should be pursued concurrently. The accuracy of automated
electronic reporting can be improved now with the technologies that
we currently have and can be iteratively reﬁned with newer technol-
ogies over time.
As quality measurement evolves in this electronic era, it is im-
portant to ensure that automated reports accurately reﬂect the health
care provided. Patients and providers will increasingly depend on that.
Lisa M. Kern, MD, MPH

Discontinuation of Statins in Routine Care Settings
TO THE EDITOR: We read Zhang and colleagues’ article (1), which
concludes that statin-related adverse events are tolerable and that
patients should be rechallenged with statins, with great interest.
Drawing such conclusions from observational studies may be lim-
ited, because the safety, efﬁcacy, and effects of withdrawing statins
were not considered in this setting.
Although statin rechallenge may be justiﬁed for some patients, it
may not be appropriate for those with limited evidence of statin
efﬁcacy and well-documented risk for harm, such as older patients
(2). In persons older than 75 years, the role of statins in primary
prevention of cardiovascular disease is unclear and evidence that they
are effective as secondary prevention is limited (2, 3). In contrast,
strong evidence from well-designed observational studies suggests
that statins are associated with adverse effects in older persons (2).
Letters

Indeed, younger patients may also experience statin-related ad-
verse effects. A recent randomized trial done in this subgroup sug-
gests that, compared with placebo, statins are associated with energy
loss and worsening exertional fatigue over 6 months (4). Therefore, it
would beneﬁt clinicians to know whether the occurrence of statin-
related adverse events differs across age groups, as well as across sex
and clinical characteristics. It is interesting that the authors did not
consider these factors, which are commonly investigated in studies of
this type.
Finally, there are beneﬁts to stopping statins. A recent pilot
study investigating statin withdrawal showed that statin reduction is
feasible, is safe, and is associated with improvements in cognitive
function in patients with Alzheimer disease (5). Improvements in
cognition, measured using Mini-Mental State Examination scores,
were observed with statin withdrawal. More important, rechallenge
with statins was associated with a signiﬁcant decrease in Mini-Mental
State Examination scores of 1.9 (P  0.007). Rechallenging patients
with statins may not always be necessary, particularly for those with
limited evidence from randomized clinical trials of beneﬁt and well-
documented observational evidence of harm.

TO THE EDITOR: As Zhang and colleagues (1) show, discontinuation
of statins in routine care settings is common. Increased liver enzyme
levels and perceived adverse effects are frequent reasons for discon-
tinuation. Yet, sometimes statin therapy is the best treatment option
for hyperlipidemia in patients with these abnormalities and prior
statin-associated adverse effects.
A 63-year-old woman was diagnosed at age 50 years with severe
hyperlipidemia; her total cholesterol levels were 400 to 500 mg/dL
(10.36 to 12.95 mmol/L). Her parents, 3 sisters, and brother had
hyperlipidemia. Her father died at age 54 years of a myocardial
infarction; her mother had survived 2 cerebral vascular accidents; and
her brother had already had 2 myocardial infarctions, the ﬁrst at age
46 years.
She initially received atorvastatin, but her physicians discontin-
ued this agent 4 years ago because of markedly increased liver en-
zyme levels. Autoimmune hepatitis was diagnosed and treated with
prednisone. Review of her liver disease suggested an overlap syn-
drome of autoimmune and cholestatic hepatitis; therefore, ursode-
oxycholic acid therapy was added to treat the cholestatic component
of her liver disease. Liver enzyme levels decreased, but total choles-
terol levels remained unchanged.
Atorvastatin was restarted, but she experienced diffuse muscle
discomfort in her arms and legs and stopped the medication. Liver
enzyme levels remained mildly elevated. The patient adamantly re-
fused to receive further statin therapy.
Given the degree of hyperlipidemia and the family history, an
n-of-1 trial was proposed to the patient; she agreed (2). Four bottles
(each containing 28 capsules), 2 with placebo and 2 with simvasta-
tin, 10 mg, were given in random order to the patient; both patient
and physician were blinded to the contents. The patient maintained
a notebook of symptoms, and liver enzyme and lipid levels were
measured every 4 weeks; only the physician was allowed to see the
results. After 4 months, treatment was unblinded and test results
showed that liver enzyme levels remained unchanged, cholesterol
levels had decreased markedly during the treatment phase, and symp-
toms were unrelated to treatment and worse when the patient re-
ceived placebo.
Given these results, the patient agreed to restart simvastatin
with a gradual dose increase until a normal cholesterol level was
achieved; at the same time, her liver levels gradually normalized. She
has received simvastatin for 10 years with no evidence of cardiovas-
cular disease or progression of liver disease.
This case shows that statins can be reintroduced in patients with
known liver disease, abnormal liver enzyme levels, and prior statin-
associated adverse effects. An n-of-1 trial in these patients can con-
vince them as well as physicians of the feasibility, safety, and beneﬁt
of statin therapy (2).
Piet C. de Groen, MD
Mayo Clinic College of Medicine
Rochester, Minnesota

TO THE EDITOR: Zhang and colleagues (1) describe the frequency
and nature of statin discontinuation at 2 large academic medical
centers. The observed discontinuation rate was quite high, with more
than 50% of patients stopping these agents at some point during the
8-year study. The article and accompanying editorial suggest that
Letters

this problem should be systematically resolved (2). However, discon-
tinuation of statins may be appropriate in certain settings.
A growing literature points toward the potentially problematic
nature of statin use, such as increased symptomatic adverse effects
and contribution to polypharmacy, in the setting of advanced or
serious comorbid illness. There is a strong aggregate history of clin-
ical trials to study the incremental beneﬁt of adding new preventive
medications; we need a similar approach to understanding if and
when to discontinue those same medications.
In a recent study evaluating the effect of thoughtful discontin-
uation of medications in the setting of advanced illness and multiple
comorbid conditions, discontinuation was associated with global im-
provement in health (3). Whether to continue or discontinue statins
in hospice and palliative care settings has been actively debated, ac-
knowledging that statins may pose more risk than beneﬁt because
longer-term gains are less likely to be realized near the end of life.
Practice varies widely; true clinical equipoise exists. In response, the
National Institute of Nursing Research–funded Palliative Care Re-
search Cooperative Group is conducting a randomized, controlled
trial of statin discontinuation in advanced illness; accrual was re-
cently completed (4). This is the ﬁrst of a planned series of studies to
understand the safety and timing of intentional medication discon-
tinuation in the setting of advanced illness—a question that needs as
much careful attention as medication initiation.

1. Zhang H, Plutzky J, Skentzos S, Morrison F, Mar P, Shubina M, et al. Discontin-

526-34. [PMID: 23546564]
2. Grundy SM. Statin discontinuation and intolerance: the challenge of lifelong ther-
apy [Editorial]. Ann Intern Med. 2013;158:562-3. [PMID: 23546569]
3. Garﬁnkel D, Mangin D. Feasibility study of a systematic approach for discontinu-
ation of multiple medications in older adults: addressing polypharmacy. Arch Intern
Med. 2010;170:1648-54. [PMID: 20937924]
4. Leblanc TW, Kutner JS, Ko D, Wheeler JL, Bull J, Abernethy AP. Developing the
evidence base for palliative care: formation of the palliative care research cooperative
and its ﬁrst trial. Hosp Pract (1995). 2010;38:137-43. [PMID: 20890063]
IN RESPONSE: We agree with Dr. Gnjidic and colleagues that the
balance of risks and beneﬁts of statin treatment must be carefully
weighed in every patient and might differ among subgroups. To
provide further guidance on treatment of dyslipidemia in older per-
sons, we examined statin discontinuation in patients older than 75
years at study entry.
There were 19 185 (9.3%) patients older than 75 years out of
the total 107 835 patients included in our study. Among these pa-
tients, 2955 (15.4%) had documented statin-related events. Of
these, 1747 (59.1%) discontinued statins at least temporarily and
910 (52.1%) were rechallenged with a statin over the subsequent 12
months.
Similar to the overall cohort, the overwhelming majority (823
patients or 90.4%) of those who were rechallenged were still receiv-
ing a statin 12 months after the original statin-related event. In
conjunction with dedicated clinical trials and meta-analyses that
showed improvements in cardiovascular outcomes and mortality in
older patients (1, 2), these data provide reassurance that older pa-
tients can both beneﬁt from and tolerate statins.
Many clinicians, including ourselves, have experienced ﬁrsthand
the difﬁculty of ascertaining the exact cause of symptoms experi-
enced by patients receiving statins. Although epidemiologic data can
illuminate the health of populations, the decision of whether to ad-
minister a statin has to be made at the individual-patient level. In the
most difﬁcult situations, a carefully designed n-of-1 experiment like
that described by Dr. de Groen can be invaluable in allowing phy-
sicians to discern between common nonspeciﬁc symptoms and an
adverse reaction to a medication in a high-risk patient.
As Dr. LeBlanc and colleagues correctly identify, patients with
many noncardiovascular comorbid conditions can present a particu-
larly difﬁcult dilemma for a clinician who needs to balance the risks
for adverse reactions and drug–drug interactions stemming from
polypharmacy against beneﬁts that could be curtailed by shorter life
expectancy. We look forward to the results of the trial that the
authors are conducting to help provide evidence-based guidance in
these complicated clinical situations.
Huabing Zhang, MD

OBSERVATION
Successful Treatment of the Postpartum Atypical Hemolytic
Uremic Syndrome With Eculizumab
Background: Thrombocytopenia with intravascular hemolysis is
a serious complication of pregnancy. When it occurs in the second
and third trimesters, it is usually associated with near-absent levels of
the ADAMTS13 protease that cleaves von Willebrand factor, a con-
dition that is typical of idiopathic thrombotic thrombocytopenic
purpura (1). During pregnancy, approximately 50% of cases of
thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura result in perinatal fetal loss
and maternal mortality is also substantial, although plasma exchange
has reduced maternal mortality from 58% before 1980 to 9% after
1996 (1). In contrast, when thrombocytopenia with intravascular
hemolysis occurs in the postpartum period, ADAMTS13 activity is
normal, and end-stage renal failure occurs within months in nearly
all patients and is not prevented by plasma exchanges. This condition
is known as the postpartum atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
(p-aHUS), and most patients have mutations in proteins of the al-
ternative complement pathway, usually affecting complement factor
H (2).
Objective: To report what we believe is the ﬁrst successful treat-
ment of the p-aHUS with eculizumab, an inhibitor of complement
pathway activation.
Case Report: Physicians transferred a 31-year-old woman to our
hospital 3 days after vaginal delivery of a healthy girl at 41 weeks’
gestation. The delivery was complicated by postpartum hemorrhage.
The mother developed hypertension, thrombocytopenia, delirium,
and acute oliguric renal failure.
Laboratory studies at our hospital found Coombs-negative in-
travascular hemolysis with schistocytes (hemoglobin level, 66 g/L
[Appendix Figure, available at www.annals.org]), and we treated the
patient with plasma exchanges, prednisone therapy, and hemodialy-
sis. Further work-up revealed normal ADAMTS13 activity and nor-
mal plasma levels of CH50, C3, C4, and complement factor H.
Complement factor I levels were decreased (19  103 g/L [normal,
21 to 46  103 g/L]). After 18 days, 27 plasma exchanges, and 9
dialysis treatments, the platelet count was 88  109 cells/L and the
serum creatinine level remained elevated (Appendix Figure).
We initiated therapy with eculizumab, an inhibitor of terminal
pathway complement activation, and administered it weekly for 4
weeks and then every 2 weeks (Appendix Figure). Platelet count
increased, kidney function recovered, and no more hemodialysis
treatments or plasma exchanges were performed. The patient had full
clinical resolution of thrombotic microangiopathy and a favorable
renal outcome (serum creatinine level, 88 mol/L [1.0 mg/dL]).
Genomic analysis found a novel heterozygous frame shift mutation
in complement factor I exon 6 (c.786delA) leading to the introduc-
tion of a new stop codon (p.Gly263AlafsX37).
Discussion: The postpartum atypical hemolytic uremic syn-
drome occurs when infection or hemorrhage triggers activation of
the alternative complement pathway and normal regulation of com-
plement activity cannot occur because of mutations in complement
factor H, complement factor I, membrane cofactor protein, or C3.
Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets C5 to prevent
activation of the terminal membrane attack complex and thus slows
complement activity. This agent has been used for aHUS not occur-
ring in the postpartum period (for example, in the prophylaxis and
treatment of recurrent posttransplant HUS and in the 2011 outbreak
in Europe of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli infection) (3–5). To
our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst description of eculizumab use in a
patient with p-aHUS. On the basis of our experience and in view of
the otherwise poor prognosis, we believe that clinicians should con-
sider eculizumab for patients with this condition.
